unit-sci-molcomp.title: Chemistry · 4 Molecules and Compounds
unit-sci-molcomp.srcName: molecules and compounds.pdf (Science 4 · Molecules and Compounds lesson check, Drive)

summary.text: The four words for what a substance is made of, and how they pair: an atom is one particle, an element is one kind of atom, a molecule is atoms joined, and a compound is different elements joined. Every substance gets two of the four. Also how to read a chemical formula: capital letters count the elements, small numbers count the atoms.

why.text: These four words are how chemists describe everything there is, and they are the groundwork for the periodic table. Once you can read a formula, H₂O stops being a code and starts saying exactly what is inside it.

objectives.text: Say what an atom, an element, a molecule and a compound are.
Name the two words that describe a substance, from its formula.
Count the elements in a formula from its capital letters.
Count the atoms in a formula from its small numbers.
Explain why every compound is a molecule but not every molecule is a compound.

parentNote.text:
Built from the completed Molecules and Compounds lesson check (one page, twelve substances, each with two answers).

It was read for the QUESTIONS it asks, not to mark the answers, so nothing here is a correction and nothing about how it went is recorded anywhere. The unit covers the one skill the paper tests twelve times: naming the two words that fit a substance. Its own twelve substances appear on the cards as examples; the graded questions use fresh ones (He, O₂, CO₂, Fe, Cl₂, CH₄, O₃, H₂O₂ and others).

ONE THING THE SHEET LEANS ON WITHOUT SAYING, added here as cards flagged as ours rather than the class's: how to read a formula. The paper expects her to know that NaOH is three elements and H₂ is one, but never says that capital letters count elements and small numbers count atoms.

A NUANCE FOR LATER GRADES: NaCl, NaOH, K₂S and CaSO₄ are ionic compounds, and a chemist would not strictly call them molecules. The sheet says every item has two answers, so its framing is molecule and compound, and the unit teaches that. No graded question depends on the difference.

nextUp.text: Start with the card that gives every substance two words. Two questions decide the pair: how many atoms, then how many kinds.

cards.def:
**The smallest piece of an element that is still that element.**
• One single particle, on its own
• Cut a piece of aluminum in half again and again, and the last piece that is still aluminum is one aluminum atom
cards.hint: Atom is the one. One particle, nothing joined to it.

cards.def:
**A substance made of only ONE kind of atom.**
• It can be single atoms, like Na (sodium) or W (tungsten)
• Or atoms of that one kind joined together, like H₂ (hydrogen gas)
• Every element has its own symbol and its own box on the periodic table
cards.hint: One kind. However many atoms there are, they are all the same.

cards.def:
**Two or more atoms joined together.**
• The atoms can be the SAME kind, like the two hydrogens in H₂
• Or DIFFERENT kinds, like the hydrogens and oxygen in H₂O
• A single atom on its own is never a molecule
cards.hint: Molecule means joined. At least two atoms, holding on to each other.

cards.def:
**Two or more DIFFERENT elements joined together.**
• Water, H₂O, is hydrogen and oxygen joined
• If every atom in it is the same kind, it is not a compound, however many atoms there are
cards.hint: Compound means a combination of different kinds.

cards.def:
**One atom alone: atom and element. Same kind joined: element and molecule. Different kinds joined: molecule and compound.**
• First ask: is it one atom, or are atoms joined?
• Then ask: is there one kind of atom, or more than one?
• Those two answers always give you the pair
cards.hint: Two questions, two words. How many atoms, then how many kinds.

cards.def:
**A symbol with no small number after it, standing on its own.**
• Na (sodium), W (tungsten), Al (aluminum), B (boron), Mg (magnesium)
• One atom, so it is an atom; one kind, so it is an element
cards.hint: Just a symbol, nothing joined. The easiest pair to spot.

cards.def:
**One kind of atom, with more than one of them joined.**
• H₂ (hydrogen gas) and N₂ (nitrogen gas)
• Joined, so it is a molecule; all one kind, so it is still an element
cards.hint: One capital letter and a small number after it.

cards.def:
**Different kinds of atom, joined.**
• H₂O (water), NaCl (table salt), K₂S, NaOH, CaSO₄
• Joined, so it is a molecule; more than one kind, so it is a compound
cards.hint: Two or more capital letters means two or more kinds.

cards.term: Every compound is a molecule, not the other way round
cards.def:
**Every compound is a molecule, but not every molecule is a compound.**
• A compound is atoms joined, so it is always a molecule too
• H₂ is a molecule, but both atoms are hydrogen, so it is not a compound
cards.hint: Compound is the pickier word. It needs joined AND different.

cards.def:
**Every capital letter in a formula starts a new element.**
• A small letter belongs to the capital in front of it: Na is ONE element, sodium
• NaOH has three capitals, N, O and H, so three elements: sodium, oxygen, hydrogen
• Count the capitals and you know how many kinds of atom there are
cards.hint: Big letter, new element. Small letter, same element.

cards.def:
**A small number after a symbol tells you how many atoms of that element there are.**
• No number means one
• H₂O is 2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen = 3 atoms
• CaSO₄ is 1 calcium + 1 sulfur + 4 oxygen = 6 atoms, of 3 kinds
cards.hint: The little number belongs to the letter just before it.

cards.def:
**Co is cobalt, one element. CO is carbon monoxide, two elements joined.**
• Co has one capital, so it is one element
• CO has two capitals, C for carbon and O for oxygen
• This is why a second letter is always written small
cards.hint: Count the capitals. That one detail changes the whole substance.

cards.def:
**Some elements are found as two atoms joined: hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen and chlorine.**
• Written H₂, N₂, O₂ and Cl₂
• They are molecules, but still elements, because both atoms are the same kind
cards.hint: Two of the same is still one kind.

cards.def:
**A compound behaves completely differently from the elements it is made of.**
• Sodium is a soft metal that reacts wildly with water; chlorine is a poisonous gas
• Joined, they make table salt, which you sprinkle on food
• Water is made of two gases, hydrogen and oxygen, and it is a liquid
cards.hint: Joined elements do not keep their old personalities.

cards.term: Symbols that do not match the name
cards.def:
**Some symbols come from an older name for the element.**
• Na is sodium, from its Latin name natrium
• K is potassium (kalium), Fe is iron (ferrum)
• W is tungsten, from its other name, wolfram
cards.hint: If the letters do not fit the English name, the name is older than English.

questions.q: What is an atom?
opts: The smallest piece of an element that is still that element
Two or more atoms of different kinds joined together
A mixture of several substances stirred into one container
Any substance that has a small number written in its formula
questions.hint: Think of the very last piece you could cut off and still have the same stuff.
steps: An atom is a single particle.
It is the smallest piece that is still that element.
Atoms joined together are a molecule, not an atom.
So an atom is the smallest piece of an element that is still that element.

ex.main: **The smallest piece of an element that is still that element.** Atoms joined together make a molecule, and different kinds joined make a compound. An atom is the single particle all of those are built from.
ex.tip: Atom is the one. Everything else in this lesson is atoms joined.

questions.q: What do you call a substance that is made of only ONE kind of atom?
questions.hint: It is the word that each box on the periodic table stands for.
steps: The substance has only one kind of atom in it.
A compound needs at least two different kinds, so it is not that.
A mixture and a solution both mean several substances stirred together.
A substance of only one kind of atom is an element.

ex.main: **An element.** It does not matter how many atoms there are. Hydrogen gas has two atoms joined, and it is still an element because both are hydrogen.
ex.tip: One kind of atom, one element.

questions.q: What do you call two or more DIFFERENT elements joined together?
questions.hint: The word means a combination of different kinds.
steps: The atoms are joined, so this is not a loose mixture.
They are different kinds, so it is not a single element.
It is more than one atom, so it is not an atom.
Different elements joined together make a compound.

ex.main: **A compound.** Water is the most famous one: hydrogen and oxygen joined. A mixture is different, because its parts are only stirred together and can be separated again without breaking anything apart.
ex.tip: Joined and different. Both have to be true.

questions.q: In a chemical formula, what does a small number after a symbol tell you?
opts: Which row of the periodic table the element is in
How many different elements are in the substance
How heavy one atom of that element is
How many atoms of that element there are
questions.hint: Look at H₂O. What is there two of?
steps: In H₂O the small 2 sits after the H.
It means there are two hydrogen atoms.
The O has no number, so there is one oxygen atom.
So the small number counts the atoms of the element just before it.

ex.main: **How many atoms of that element there are.** The number of different elements comes from counting the capital letters instead. No small number at all means there is just one atom.
ex.tip: The little number belongs to the letter in front of it.

questions.q: Helium is written He. Which two words describe it?
questions.hint: Is there anything joined to it?
steps: He is one symbol with no small number after it.
So it is a single atom, with nothing joined to it.
Only one kind of atom is there, so it is an element.
One atom, one kind: atom and element.

ex.main: **Atom and element.** A single atom on its own is always both. It cannot be a molecule, because nothing is joined to it, and it cannot be a compound, because there is only one kind.
ex.tip: Just a symbol, nothing joined: atom and element.

questions.q: The oxygen you breathe is written O₂. Which two words describe it?
questions.hint: Count the atoms, then count the kinds.
steps: The small 2 means two oxygen atoms.
Two atoms joined together make a molecule.
Both atoms are oxygen, so there is only one kind.
One kind of atom means it is an element: element and molecule.

ex.main: **Element and molecule.** It is joined, so it is a molecule. But both atoms are oxygen, so it is still an element, not a compound.
ex.tip: Two of the same is still one kind.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide is written CO₂. Which two words describe it?
questions.hint: How many capital letters are there?
steps: C and O are two capital letters, so there are two elements: carbon and oxygen.
The atoms are joined, so it is a molecule.
Different elements joined together make a compound.
So it is a molecule and a compound.

ex.main: **Molecule and compound.** Carbon and oxygen are two different elements, joined. That makes it a compound, and every compound is a molecule too.
ex.tip: Two capitals, two kinds. Different kinds joined is a compound.

questions.q: Iron is written Fe. Which two words describe it?
questions.hint: One letter is a capital and one is small. What does that mean?
steps: Fe has one capital letter, F, so it is one element.
The small e belongs to the F; it is not a second element.
There is no small number, so it is one atom.
One atom, one kind: atom and element.

ex.main: **Atom and element.** Two letters do not mean two elements. Only a capital letter starts a new element, and the small e is part of iron's symbol.
ex.tip: Count capitals, not letters.

questions.q: Chlorine gas is written Cl₂. Which two words describe it?
questions.hint: Two letters, one capital, then a small number.
steps: Cl has one capital, so it is one element: chlorine.
The small 2 means two chlorine atoms.
Two atoms joined make a molecule.
Both are chlorine, so it stays an element: element and molecule.

ex.main: **Element and molecule.** Chlorine is one of the elements found as joined pairs, like hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen. Joined makes it a molecule, but one kind keeps it an element.
ex.tip: One capital and a small number: element and molecule.

questions.q: Methane, the gas burned on a kitchen stove, is written CH₄. Which two words describe it?
questions.hint: How many capital letters, and are the atoms joined?
steps: C and H are two capitals, so two elements: carbon and hydrogen.
The 4 means four hydrogen atoms, joined to the carbon.
Atoms joined make a molecule.
Different elements joined make a compound: molecule and compound.

ex.main: **Molecule and compound.** It has 5 atoms of 2 kinds. The number of atoms does not decide it; the number of KINDS does.
ex.tip: Two capitals is enough to make a compound.

questions.q: Ammonia is written NH₃. How many atoms are in one molecule of it?
questions.hint: Count every atom, including the ones with no number.
steps: N has no small number, so there is 1 nitrogen atom.
H has a 3 after it, so there are 3 hydrogen atoms.
So one molecule has 4 atoms.

ex.main: **4.** One nitrogen and three hydrogen. Answering 3 forgets the nitrogen, because it has no number written after it, and answering 2 counts the kinds of element instead of the atoms.
ex.tip: No number means one. It still counts.

questions.q: Sugar (glucose) is written C₆H₁₂O₆. How many different ELEMENTS are in it?
questions.hint: The question asks for kinds of atom, not how many atoms.
steps: Count the capital letters: C, H and O.
Each capital starts a new element: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
The small numbers count atoms, which is a different question.
So there are 3 elements.

ex.main: **3.** Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. There are 24 atoms in all, but that answers how many atoms, not how many kinds.
ex.tip: Elements: count the capitals. Atoms: add the numbers.

questions.q: Co is cobalt and CO is carbon monoxide. Which one is a compound, and why?
opts: CO, because its two capital letters are two different elements
Co, because its two letters stand for two different elements
Both, because each one is written with exactly two letters
Neither, because a compound always needs a small number
questions.hint: Look at which letters are capitals.
steps: Co has one capital, C, and a small o that belongs to it.
So Co is one element, cobalt.
CO has two capitals, C for carbon and O for oxygen.
Two different elements joined make a compound, so CO is the compound.

ex.main: **CO, because its two capital letters are two different elements.** Co is a single element, cobalt. A compound does not need a small number either: CO has one carbon and one oxygen, and that is enough.
ex.tip: Capitals count elements. The size of a letter changes the whole substance.

questions.q: Which statement is true?
opts: Every molecule is a compound, but not every compound is a molecule
Every compound is a molecule, but not every molecule is a compound
A molecule and a compound always mean exactly the same thing
A substance can never be both a molecule and a compound
questions.hint: Test each statement against H₂, which is two hydrogen atoms joined.
steps: A compound is different elements joined, so its atoms are joined: it is a molecule.
H₂ is atoms joined, so it is a molecule.
But both of its atoms are hydrogen, so it is not a compound.
So every compound is a molecule, but not every molecule is a compound.

ex.main: **Every compound is a molecule, but not every molecule is a compound.** H₂ is the example that proves it: a molecule made of one kind of atom, so it is not a compound.
ex.tip: Compound is the pickier word. It needs joined AND different.

questions.q: Ozone, a gas high in the sky, is written O₃. It has three atoms. Which two words describe it?
questions.hint: Three atoms is a lot. Does that make it a compound?
steps: The small 3 means three oxygen atoms, joined.
Atoms joined make a molecule.
All three are oxygen, so there is only one kind of atom.
One kind means it is an element, not a compound: element and molecule.

ex.main: **Element and molecule.** The number of atoms never makes something a compound. Only different KINDS do, and every atom in ozone is oxygen.
ex.tip: More atoms is not more kinds.

questions.q: Someone says hydrogen gas, H₂, is a compound because it has two atoms. What is wrong with that?
opts: A compound needs at least three atoms, and H₂ only has two
Nothing is wrong; any substance with two atoms is a compound
H₂ is a single atom, so it cannot be joined to anything
Both atoms are hydrogen, and a compound needs different elements
questions.hint: Two atoms tells you it is joined. What else does a compound need?
steps: H₂ has two atoms joined, so it is a molecule.
A compound needs two or more DIFFERENT elements.
Both of H₂'s atoms are hydrogen, one kind.
So it is an element and a molecule, not a compound.

ex.main: **Both atoms are hydrogen, and a compound needs different elements.** Two atoms joined only makes a molecule. Water, H₂O, is a compound because oxygen joins the hydrogen.
ex.tip: Joined makes a molecule. Different makes a compound.

questions.q: Put these in order from FEWEST atoms to MOST atoms.
questions.hint: Add up the small numbers, and count a symbol with no number as one.
steps: He has no number: 1 atom.
O₂ has a 2: 2 atoms.
H₂O is 2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen: 3 atoms.
CH₄ is 1 carbon + 4 hydrogen: 5 atoms.

ex.main: **He, O₂, H₂O, CH₄: 1, 2, 3 and 5 atoms.** Count every symbol, and count a symbol with no small number after it as one.
ex.tip: No number means one. Then add.

questions.q: Sodium is a soft metal that reacts wildly with water. Chlorine is a poisonous gas. Joined, they make table salt, which is safe to eat. What does this show?
opts: A compound has its own properties, different from the elements in it
A compound keeps all the properties of the elements in it
Table salt must be a mixture, because its elements can be tasted
Elements only change when they are melted down together
questions.hint: Compare what salt is like with what sodium and chlorine are like.
steps: Sodium is a dangerous metal on its own.
Chlorine is a poisonous gas on its own.
Salt is neither: it is a safe white solid.
So joining elements makes something with new properties of its own.

ex.main: **A compound has its own properties, different from the elements in it.** That is the big difference between a compound and a mixture. Stir sand and iron filings together and each keeps acting the way it always did; join sodium and chlorine and you get something new.
ex.tip: Joined elements make something new.

questions.q: Which of these formulas CANNOT be a compound?
questions.hint: A compound needs at least two different elements. Count the capitals in each.
steps: S₈ has one capital, S, so it has one element: sulfur.
HCl has two capitals, H and C: hydrogen and chlorine.
NO₂ has N and O, and CO has C and O.
Only S₈ has a single kind of atom, so it cannot be a compound.

ex.main: **S₈.** It has eight atoms, but they are all sulfur, so it is an element and a molecule. Each of the others has two capital letters, so two elements joined.
ex.tip: A big number does not make a compound. A second capital does.

questions.q: Hydrogen peroxide, used to clean a cut, is written H₂O₂. Which two words describe it?
questions.hint: It has the same two letters as water. Count the kinds of atom.
steps: H and O are two capitals, so two elements: hydrogen and oxygen.
The atoms are joined, so it is a molecule.
Different elements joined make a compound.
So it is a molecule and a compound, just like water.

ex.main: **Molecule and compound.** It has one more oxygen than water, which makes it a different substance, but it is still two kinds of atom joined.
ex.tip: Different numbers, different substance. Same kinds, same pair of words.

sorts.title: One kind of atom, or different kinds joined?

items.why: Two atoms, but both oxygen: one kind.
Two capitals, carbon and oxygen: two kinds joined.
One capital, F. The small e belongs to it.
Carbon and hydrogen: two kinds joined.
Nitrogen and hydrogen: two kinds joined.
Three atoms, but every one is oxygen.
Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen: three kinds joined.
One capital, C, with a small o. One kind of atom.
Two capitals, C and O: carbon and oxygen joined.
Two chlorine atoms joined are still only chlorine.
Hydrogen and oxygen, the same two kinds as water.
